name: Workplace Skills and Productivity
objectives: Given a real work situation, write a short, clear, professional email or text with AI help, with the main point in the first line, a polite ending and your own voice
Given a topic to raise with a supervisor, prepare and practice a short, respectful conversation, with your point written in one sentence and practiced at least once
Given feedback or a problem at work, respond calmly and report the problem to the right person, including what happened, when and what you did
Given a list of tasks for a workday, make a to-do list sorted into must, should and could, with tasks that have a deadline today at the top
Given a link to a shared schedule or document, open it, find your part and add to it, without changing parts that are not yours
Given your workplace's AI policy, choose which work tasks you may use AI for and what information to keep out, never putting customer or company private information into an AI tool

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Writing professional messages
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short, clear, professional email or text to someone at work.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real work situation, you will write a short, clear, professional email or text with AI help, with the main point in the first line, a polite ending and your own voice.
At work, how you write matters. A professional message is short, polite and clear: it says what you need in the first line, gives a reason if needed, and ends with a thank-you.
A simple pattern: greeting, the point, one or two details, what you are asking for, thanks and your name. For example: "Hi Maria, I would like to switch my Saturday shift to Sunday this week because of a family event. I can help find someone to cover. Thank you, Andre."
An AI assistant can help: "Make this message to my supervisor more professional but still friendly." Then read it, make it sound like you, and check spelling of names. Avoid texting slang, all capital letters and too many emojis at work.
Step by step:
- Start with a greeting and the person's name.
- Say your point in the first line.
- Add one or two details.
- Say what you are asking for.
- End with thanks and your name.
Words to know:
- Professional: the respectful, clear way people communicate at work.
- Supervisor: the person who directs your work and schedule.
Try it now: Write a rough message to a supervisor asking a question about your schedule. Ask an AI assistant to make it more professional but friendly, then make one change so it sounds like you.
You can now write a short, professional message to someone at work.

check.q: What should the first line of a work message do?
check.why: Putting the main point first makes a work message quick to read.

check.q: AI made your message to a supervisor very formal and long. What would you do?
options: Ask AI to make it longer
Shorten it and change words so it sounds like you
check.why: A good work message is short, polite and in your own voice.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Talking with your supervisor
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Prepare for and hold a short, respectful conversation with a supervisor.
This lesson builds toward: Given a topic to raise with a supervisor, you will prepare and practice a short, respectful conversation, with your point written in one sentence and practiced at least once.
Some things are better said in person: asking for help, explaining a mistake, or asking about more hours. A little preparation makes it easier.
Before you talk, write down the point in one sentence and what you hope will happen. Pick a calm moment and ask, "Do you have two minutes?" Speak clearly, listen fully, and repeat back what you heard: "So you want me to finish the returns before restocking. Got it."
You can practice with AI: "Pretend you are my supervisor at a warehouse. I want to ask for more hours. Ask me questions, then give me feedback on how I did."
Step by step:
- Write your point in one sentence.
- Pick a calm moment and ask if they have a minute.
- Speak clearly and listen fully.
- Repeat back what you heard.
- Practice first with AI if you like.
Words to know:
- Repeat back: saying in your own words what someone told you, to make sure you understood.
- Role-play: practicing a conversation by acting it out.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to role-play your supervisor while you ask for more hours. Do the conversation, then ask it for two tips to do better.
You can now prepare for and hold a respectful conversation with a supervisor.

check.q: Why write your point in one sentence before talking to a supervisor?
options: So you can read it to them word for word
So you know exactly what you want to say
So you can send it instead of talking
So you can skip the conversation
check.why: One clear sentence helps you stay on point in the conversation.

check.q: Your supervisor looks busy and stressed. What would you do?
options: Ask a coworker to talk for you
Wait for a calm moment and ask if they have a minute
check.why: A calm moment and asking first shows respect and gets a better result.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Handling feedback and problems
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Respond to feedback calmly and report a problem the right way.
This lesson builds toward: Given feedback or a problem at work, you will respond calmly and report the problem to the right person, including what happened, when and what you did.
Feedback is information about how you are doing. Even when it is hard to hear, it is how people get better and get trusted with more. Listen, say thank you, ask a question if something is unclear, and show you are working on it.
Problems happen: you will be late, you made a mistake, a machine broke, a coworker is causing trouble. Report it early, to the right person, with facts: what happened, when, and what you did. "I dropped a case of glass jars in aisle 4 at 2 pm. I blocked the area and got the broom. Who should I tell for the inventory?"
If you feel angry, take a breath before answering. You can say, "Let me think about that and get back to you." Use AI to help plan a calm reply, not to send one in anger.
Step by step:
- Listen without arguing.
- Say thank you and ask questions if needed.
- Report problems early, with facts.
- Take a breath if you feel angry.
- Follow up on what you said you would do.
Words to know:
- Feedback: information about how you are doing, to help you improve.
- Report: telling the right person what happened.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "My supervisor said I need to work faster on the line. Help me plan a calm, positive reply and two ways to improve." Write down the reply you would use.
You can now respond to feedback calmly and report a problem clearly.

options: Information about how you are doing
A complaint from a customer only
check.why: Feedback is information about how you are doing so you can improve.

check.q: You dropped a box and broke what was inside. What would you do?
options: Hide it and hope no one finds it
Report it early to the right person with the facts
Wait until the end of the week
check.why: Reporting early and with facts shows honesty and helps fix the problem.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Planning and prioritizing your workday
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a to-do list and put the most important tasks first.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of tasks for a workday, you will make a to-do list sorted into must, should and could, with tasks that have a deadline today at the top.
A to-do list keeps you from forgetting tasks and helps you do the most important ones first. That is called prioritizing.
Write every task. Then mark each: Must do today (deadlines, safety, what your supervisor asked for), Should do, and Could do if there is time. Start with the must-do tasks. If you are unsure what matters most, ask your supervisor; that is a smart question, not a weakness.
AI can help sort a list: "Here are my tasks for my shift at a grocery store. Put them in order of importance and explain why." Check its order against what your supervisor said.
Step by step:
- Write every task.
- Mark each: must, should or could.
- Do the must-do tasks first.
- Ask your supervisor if unsure.
- Check off tasks as you finish.
Words to know:
- Prioritize: to decide which tasks are most important and do them first.
- Deadline: the time by which something must be done.
Try it now: Write six tasks from a real or imagined shift. Mark each must, should or could. Ask an AI assistant to put them in order, and compare with your own order.
You can now plan a workday and do the most important tasks first.

check.q: In a must, should, could list, which tasks go under "must"?
options: Tasks that have to be done today
check.why: Must tasks are the ones that have to be done today, often with a deadline.

check.q: Two tasks both seem urgent and you are not sure which comes first. What would you do?
options: Ask your supervisor which matters most
check.why: When unsure what is most important, you ask your supervisor.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Shared schedules and documents
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Open a shared schedule or document, find your part, and add to it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a link to a shared schedule or document, you will open it, find your part and add to it, without changing parts that are not yours.
Many jobs share schedules and documents online. Your shifts may be in a scheduling app your employer picks; checklists and forms may be in Google Docs, Google Sheets, Microsoft Word or Excel.
When someone shares a document, you get a link by email or text. Tap it, sign in if asked, and find your part. You can type into the document, and others see the changes. A comment lets you ask a question without changing the text: select the words and choose Comment.
Check your schedule app daily, and if a shift changes, confirm with your supervisor. Never change something in a shared document that is not yours to change; ask first.
Step by step:
- Tap the shared link from email or text.
- Sign in if asked.
- Find your part of the document or schedule.
- Type your update, or add a comment to ask a question.
- Check your schedule daily and confirm changes.
Words to know:
- Shared document: a file online that several people can open and edit.
- Comment: a note added beside the text, used to ask or answer questions.
Try it now: Create a free Google Doc or Word document called "My work week". Type your shifts for a week, add one comment as a question, and practice sharing it by link with a family member or yourself.
You can now use shared schedules and documents and add to them properly.

check.q: How do you usually get into a shared document?
options: By a link sent by email or text
check.why: When a document is shared with you, you usually get a link.

check.q: You see a mistake in a coworker's part of a shared schedule. What would you do?
options: Add a comment or ask them about it
check.why: You do not change parts that are not yours; you comment or ask first.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Using AI at work the right way
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Follow your workplace's AI rules and keep company and customer information private.
This lesson builds toward: Given your workplace's AI policy, you will choose which work tasks you may use AI for and what information to keep out, never putting customer or company private information into an AI tool.
Many workplaces use AI, and many have rules about it. Some allow certain tools; some do not allow AI at all for some tasks. Always ask your supervisor what is allowed before you use AI for work.
Never put private work information into a public AI tool: customer names, addresses or payment details, coworkers' information, prices or plans that are not public, or passwords. That can break company rules and the law.
Use AI for things like improving your own writing, explaining a word, or practicing a conversation. Check what it says, and be honest if you used it for something you hand in.
Step by step:
- Ask your supervisor what AI use is allowed.
- Never put customer, coworker or company private information into AI.
- Use AI for your own writing and learning.
- Check its answers.
- Be honest about using it.
Words to know:
- Confidential: private information that must not be shared outside the company.
- Policy: a written rule at a workplace.
Try it now: Final task: ask an AI assistant to help write a short, professional message to a supervisor asking to switch one shift, with a reason and an offer to help find coverage. Make it sound like you and check it has no private details. Then make a prioritized to-do list for a workday.
You can now communicate professionally, plan your work, use shared tools, and use AI at work the right way.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear request The message does not say which shift or why, or the point is buried. The first line asks to switch a named shift, with a short reason. It is short enough to read in a few seconds and ends with thanks and your name. Offer to help No offer to help find coverage. Offers to help find someone to cover the shift. Names a possible coworker or a time to talk about it. Sounds like you, private details out Uses words the learner would not say, or has private details. Polite, in the learner's own words, with no private details. The learner changed some AI words themselves and can say why. Prioritized to-do list Tasks are in no order, or deadline tasks are not first. Tasks are sorted into must, should and could, with today's deadlines first. Also notes who to ask if priorities are unclear. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.why: A policy is a written rule your workplace expects you to follow.

check.q: You want AI to help reply to a customer complaint that includes their phone number. What would you do?
options: Paste it all into a public AI tool
Check the AI policy and leave out the customer's details
Post the complaint online for advice
Send the customer's number to a friend
check.why: Follow your workplace's AI rules and keep customer information private.
